periods.activity_title: Defining Work Using Force and Displacement in Direction
periods.section_anchor: 7.1 Work Done by a Constant Force
periods.visual_aids: Force-displacement graph drawn on board showing area = work done

time_bands.activity: Open with the wheat-bag scenario from the chapter: ask students which case involves more work — lifting one bag to 1 m or two bags to 1 m, or one bag to 2 m. Invite brief responses and note the two variables students identify: force and displacement.

Establish the formal definition W = F × s, emphasising 'displacement in the direction of force'. Work through the unit derivation: 1 J = 1 N × 1 m. Introduce the force-displacement graph on the board and demonstrate that the area under a horizontal line (constant force) equals work done, then ask students how they would find work if the line were not horizontal.

Students individually attempt two numerical problems: (a) calculate work done lifting a 5 kg bag (take g = 10 m s⁻²) through 1.5 m, and (b) read the area under a simple trapezoidal force-displacement graph drawn on the board. Pairs compare answers and resolve discrepancies.

Whole-class debrief: highlight that 'force in the direction of displacement' is the key qualifier. Students write one sentence in their notebooks distinguishing the everyday meaning of work from the scientific one, using the wheat-bag context.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit is the chapter's entry point, so ground every example in the familiar wheat-bag scenario before moving to symbols. A common early error is students multiplying total force by displacement without checking direction alignment — press on 'displacement in the direction of force' each time you write the formula. Close by checking that students can read area off the force-displacement graph before moving on.
homework: A person pushes a 20 kg box horizontally with a force of 40 N over 3 m. Calculate the work done and sketch the force-displacement graph for this situation.

periods.activity_title: Identifying Three Conditions That Make Scientific Work Zero
periods.section_anchor: 7.1.1 When is work done equal to zero?
materials: Printed scenario cards (one set per pair)
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram showing three cases: zero force, zero displacement, force perpendicular to displacement

time_bands.activity: Pose the question: 'A weightlifter holds a 100 kg barbell motionless above their head for 10 seconds. Have they done any work on the barbell?' Students write a yes/no prediction with a reason before any discussion.

Distribute scenario cards, each describing a physical situation (pushing a wall, carrying a bag horizontally, lifting a book). Pairs decide whether scientific work is zero or non-zero and write the condition that makes it zero. Groups share and the class builds the three-condition list on the board.

Return to the weightlifter prediction. Students revise their reasoning using the zero-displacement condition. Extend to the 'Pause and Ponder' coin-friction case: does friction on a sliding coin do positive, negative, or zero work? Students reason in writing, then discuss.

Teacher draws the perpendicular-force diagram (box carried horizontally, upward force arrow, horizontal displacement arrow). Students classify five further situations on the board — each student assigns a condition number. Close with the muscle-exhaustion contrast: the body's internal energy decreases even when scientific work on the object is zero.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established W = F × s, students now encounter its limits; the biggest conceptual hurdle is the perpendicular case, where effort is real but scientific work is zero. Watch for students confusing 'the person does no work on the bag' with 'no energy is spent' — the muscle-exhaustion distinction directly addresses this. The coin-friction question is a good readiness check: students who correctly say friction does negative work on the coin (opposing motion) are ready to move to the next section.

periods.activity_title: Calculating Positive and Negative Work in Direction-Based Scenarios
periods.visual_aids: Board diagrams showing force and displacement arrows for dumbbell lift/lower and goalkeeper scenario

time_bands.activity: Draw a dumbbell on the board. Ask: 'The girl lifts it up, then lowers it back to the start. Are both actions work? Is it the same amount?' Students predict, then the class works through the sign rule: same direction → positive; opposite direction → negative.

Work through the goalkeeper example step by step: force = 200 N directed opposite to ball's displacement of 15 cm = 0.15 m, so W = –(200 × 0.15) = –30 J. Students replicate the calculation independently, then the teacher introduces Newton's third law angle: simultaneously, the ball does +30 J of work on the goalkeeper's hands.

Students solve three problems in pairs: (a) a braking car where friction opposes motion, (b) gravity on a ball thrown upward (negative), and (c) gravity on the same ball falling back down (positive). Each pair writes the force and displacement direction before computing the sign.
Pairs present one problem each. Consolidate: the sign of work encodes the energy relationship — positive work adds energy to the object, negative work removes it.

periods.teacher_notes: Building on zero-work conditions, students now assign signs; the most persistent error is treating work as always positive because force and displacement magnitudes are positive numbers. Insist that students draw force and displacement arrows before writing any equation. The Newton's-third-law note about the ball and goalkeeper doing opposite-sign work on each other often surprises students — hold that thread because it recurs in the work-energy theorem's collision example.
homework: A 0.5 kg book slides off a table and falls 0.8 m to the floor. Calculate the work done by gravity and the work done by the normal force from the table surface during the fall, giving the sign and direction reasoning for each.

periods.activity_title: Tracing Energy Transfers Through the Work-Energy Theorem
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram of carrom-board sequence: striker → white coin → black coin with force and displacement arrows

time_bands.activity: Present the cricket-ball-and-wicket scenario and the flowerpot scenario from the chapter. Ask: 'What do both objects have that lets them do work on something else?' Elicit 'energy' and define energy as the capacity to do work. State W = ΔE and its unit, joule.

Distribute the carrom worksheet. Students trace each collision in sequence — striker hits white coin, white hits black — identifying at each step: (a) which object does positive work, (b) which receives negative work, and (c) how energy transfers. Use Newton's third law to show that positive and negative work are always paired in a collision.

Students tackle the 'Pause and Ponder' bicycle question: list the energy conversions from muscular energy as a rider pedals at constant speed on a flat road (muscular → kinetic, with thermal loss to friction). Groups compare lists and refine, attending to the 'constant speed' constraint that limits kinetic energy change.

Class constructs a generalised statement: when net positive work is done on an object, its energy increases; net negative work decreases it; zero net work leaves energy unchanged. Students write this as a one-paragraph summary in their own words.

periods.teacher_notes: Having signed work established, this unit shifts from computing work to understanding what work does to an object's energy. The carrom example is the richest vehicle — watch for students who think the white coin 'loses' work rather than 'transfers energy'; redirect them to W = ΔE applied to each coin separately. The bicycle Pause-and-Ponder is a useful exit check: students who include thermal loss through friction have grasped that energy conservation holds even when mechanical energy does not.

periods.activity_title: Mapping Energy Conversions Across Forms of Energy
periods.visual_aids: Board energy-conversion web built live during discussion

time_bands.activity: Students brainstorm on sticky notes: one colour for 'devices or phenomena you know', one for 'what kind of energy change happens'. Place notes on the board without organising them yet. Prompt with the electric bulb and ringing bell examples from the chapter if the class stalls.

Class collaboratively sorts the sticky notes into the seven named forms from the chapter (mechanical, thermal, light, sound, electrical, nuclear, chemical). Draw arrows between notes to show conversions. Emphasise the food → muscle → mechanical chain and the electrical → light chain as the chapter's worked examples.

Students individually write three conversion chains not already on the board — each chain must name the starting form, converting device or process, and ending form. Pairs cross-check that named forms match the chapter's list and that conversions are physically plausible.

Connect to the chapter's scope: mechanical energy is the form this chapter analyses deeply. Students annotate their chains, circling any arrow that involves mechanical energy on either side, and note that kinetic and potential energy are its two components — to be derived in the next section.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit bridges the work-energy theorem to the chapter's mechanical energy strand; the discovery approach is well-suited here because students already have everyday exposure to energy forms. A common confusion is treating 'energy' and 'power' as synonyms — if this surfaces, note it now without resolving it fully, since power gets its own unit later. The annotation asking students to circle mechanical-energy arrows primes them for the kinetic and potential energy derivations without naming those sections.

periods.activity_title: Deriving Kinetic Energy and Applying K = ½mv² to Real Problems
periods.visual_aids: Board derivation layout: kinematics equation v² = u² + 2as alongside W = F × s = ma × s

time_bands.activity: Set up the derivation scenario: an object of mass m starts at rest (u = 0) and accelerates to velocity v under constant force F over displacement s. Write v² = u² + 2as on the board and ask students to substitute into W = F × s = ma × s, guiding them to arrive at W = ½mv² step by step.

Extend to the general case (u ≠ 0): W = ½m(v² – u²) = change in kinetic energy. Discuss sign behaviour: positive work increases K, negative work decreases K, zero work leaves K constant. Confirm there is no direction for K — it is always non-negative.

Students work through the three chapter examples: (a) velocity doubles → KE quadruples; (b) cricket ball at 154.8 km h⁻¹ (convert to m s⁻¹ first) → ≈184.9 J; (c) jet aircraft stopped by wire — use W = ΔK to find landing speed. Each student shows unit conversions explicitly.

Pause-and-Ponder: two objects with the same KE but masses m and 4m — which has greater speed? Students derive the ratio algebraically before checking numerically. Close with the constant-velocity question: does KE change with position? Students state why or why not.

periods.teacher_notes: The derivation is the conceptual core of this unit; students who lose the thread usually do so when substituting a = F/m back into the displacement expression — keep both lines visible on the board simultaneously. The velocity-doubling result (K quadruples) surprises many students and is the most common exam stumbling block, so confirm it algebraically and with numbers. The jet-aircraft problem is an excellent application of W = ΔK in reverse, finding initial velocity from known work done.
homework: A 2 kg ball is thrown horizontally at 15 m s⁻¹ and a braking force of 3 N acts on it over 20 m in the direction opposing motion. Calculate the ball's kinetic energy at the start and its speed after the braking force has acted.

periods.activity_title: Investigating Gravitational Potential Energy Through Height and Deformation
materials: Heavy ball (or large eraser as surrogate)
Tray of loose sand or soft clay
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram of Earth-ball system with height h labelled for U = mgh derivation

time_bands.activity: Introduce potential energy as stored energy due to deformation or relative position, using the rubber-band slingshot and bent-bow examples. Ask: 'Where does the arrow's kinetic energy come from?' Elicit 'stored energy in the bent bow' and connect to the broader principle of gravitational, elastic, and positional storage.

Conduct Activity 7.1: students drop the heavy ball into the sand tray from exactly 1 m and then from 2 m, measuring and recording the depth of each depression. Groups compare results and state the relationship between drop height and stored energy in one sentence.

Lead the gravitational PE derivation on the board: to raise mass m to height h at constant speed, force = mg, so W = mgh = potential energy gained. Students apply U = mgh to the chapter's worked example: 200 g ball thrown 10 m high → U = 0.2 × 10 × 10 = 20 J. They verify units throughout.

Stretch: students briefly stretch rubber bands of different lengths and qualitatively rank their stored elastic potential energy, then distinguish this elastic PE from gravitational PE — both are 'potential' but arise from different interactions. Students write one sentence defining potential energy in their own words.

periods.teacher_notes: Activity 7.1 is straightforward but needs a genuinely loose, level sand surface to show a clear depth difference — if sand is unavailable, soft clay or damp soil works. Watch for the misconception that a heavier ball dropped from the same height always makes a deeper dent regardless of height; the experiment's variable is height, not mass. The derivation's key step is that constant-speed lifting means force exactly equals mg — check that students understand why this condition is chosen.

periods.activity_title: Verifying Conservation of Mechanical Energy with a Pendulum
materials: Small heavy bob (metal nut or similar)
Clamp or door frame for suspension
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram of pendulum at three positions (height h, lowest point, height h′) with KE and PE labelled at each

time_bands.activity: Define mechanical energy as ME = K + U. Present the algebraic proof from the chapter for free fall: at height h, ME = mgh; at intermediate time t, PE drops by ½mg²t² while KE rises by ½mg²t², so ME = mgh throughout. Students confirm the algebra step by step on their notebooks.

Conduct Activity 7.2: suspend the pendulum, mark the bob's starting height on the wall, release from rest, and observe the height it reaches on the other side. Students record starting and final heights for three different release heights, noting whether ME is conserved and explaining any shortfall using friction and air resistance.

Work through the chapter's two applied problems: (a) slide of height h — using ME conservation, v at the bottom = √(2gh), independent of mass and slide shape; students verify this is independent of the path taken. (b) Truck braking problem: convert 72 km h⁻¹ to m s⁻¹, use K = work done by sand force to find ramp length of 20 m.

Pause-and-Ponder: students trace KE and PE at points along a ball roller-coaster track sketched on the board, explaining why successive peaks are lower. They write one sentence attributing the loss to friction, connecting to Activity 7.2's shortfall observation.

periods.teacher_notes: Having derived gravitational PE, this unit brings K and U together; the pendulum activity is the chapter's most direct experimental verification of conservation. A persistent misconception is that the bob should return to exactly the same height — real shortfall does not disprove conservation, it reveals energy transferred to thermal form via friction and air resistance. The slide problem's mass-independence often surprises students; confirm it by working the algebra with a specific mass and then without one.
homework: A 3 kg object is released from rest at a height of 5 m. Ignoring air resistance, calculate its kinetic energy and speed at heights of 3 m and 0 m, showing that total mechanical energy is the same at each point.

periods.activity_title: Calculating Power as Rate of Work and Comparing Scenarios
periods.visual_aids: Board table comparing walking vs. running up stairs: same work, different times, different power

time_bands.activity: Ask: 'You and a friend climb the same staircase — you run, they walk. Who does more work?' Students predict. Establish that work done is identical (same force, same height), but the rate differs. Define P = W/t and its SI unit, the watt.

Students work in groups: they estimate their own power climbing a known staircase (measure height with a tape, estimate body mass, time the climb). Each student calculates P = mgh/t and groups compare values, noting factors that cause variation. If staircase access is unavailable, students use the chapter's weightlifter worked example and the car acceleration example as the computational vehicles.

Work through the car example: 1000 kg car from rest to 72 km h⁻¹ in 10 s. Students first compute KE gained (= work done by engine), then divide by time to get 20,000 W. Discuss: the 'rate' framing means a more powerful engine can achieve the same speed change in less time.

Students create two new scenarios of their own — one where they double the power needed and one where they halve it — by adjusting either work or time in a given base scenario. Pairs exchange and verify each other's calculations. Close by confirming the watt-joule-second relationship.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established energy as the capacity to do work and conservation of mechanical energy, power introduces the time dimension — a natural progression the chapter itself makes through the staircase contrast. Watch for students who think the faster climber does more work rather than more work per unit time. The staircase activity is engaging and gives concrete numbers; if classroom logistics prevent it, the weightlifter and car examples from the chapter are fully sufficient.

periods.activity_title: Introducing Simple Machines, Effort, Load, and Mechanical Advantage
materials: Everyday objects demonstrating machines (scissors, nutcracker, broom — or pictures)
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram defining effort, load, and fulcrum on a generic simple machine

time_bands.activity: Ask students to recall (or imagine) lifting a heavy suitcase versus rolling it up a ramp — which needs less force? Establish the purpose of simple machines: they change the magnitude or direction of force applied, without reducing the total work done.

Define effort and load using a tug-of-war analogy, then introduce MA = load/effort. Show the objects (or pictures): students assign effort, load, and fulcrum to scissors, a wheelbarrow, and a pair of tweezers and compute a qualitative MA (greater than 1, equal to 1, or less than 1).

Pose the discovery challenge: 'If a machine with MA = 3 lifts a 90 N load, what effort is needed?' Students solve (30 N), then flip it: 'If effort is 50 N and MA = 2, what load can be lifted?' The class derives that MA > 1 means smaller effort than load, MA = 1 means effort equals load, and MA < 1 means effort is larger but displacement is reduced.

Students state the fundamental constraint in their own words: machines do not create energy; total work done by the machine equals work done on the load. They connect this to the work-energy theorem established earlier in the chapter, writing W_effort = W_load as the conserved equality.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the chapter's second major strand; students coming from the energy sections already have W = F × s, making the MA derivation from work conservation natural. A common confusion is thinking that a machine with MA > 1 gives 'free' extra force — make explicit from the start that a larger MA means a longer effort displacement for the same load displacement. The three machine examples (scissors, wheelbarrow, tweezers) span all three lever classes and will recur, so taking a moment to note their different MA qualities is worthwhile.

periods.activity_title: Analysing Fixed and Movable Pulleys and Deriving Mechanical Advantage
materials: Pulley wheel (or smooth rod as surrogate)
Hanging masses or water bottles of known mass
periods.visual_aids: Board diagrams of fixed pulley (MA = 1, direction change only) and movable pulley (MA > 1) with rope segments labelled

time_bands.activity: Demonstrate a fixed pulley: hang a known load and measure the effort with a spring balance. Students record load and effort values, compute MA, and confirm MA ≈ 1. Ask: 'If MA = 1, why use a fixed pulley at all?' Elicit that it changes the direction of force — pulling down is more convenient than pushing up.

Set up a movable pulley arrangement (or diagram it carefully on the board with rope-segment count). Students measure or read the effort required to lift the same load, compute MA, and compare with the fixed case. They count the number of rope segments supporting the load and relate this to the MA achieved.

Students apply the work-conservation principle: effort × effort distance = load × load distance. For a movable pulley with two supporting rope segments, they verify that the effort moves twice the distance the load moves, confirming MA = 2 without violating energy conservation.

Real-life extension: students identify the pulley principle in elevators and cranes (from the chapter). They write one sentence explaining why a crane operator might prefer a block-and-tackle (multiple movable pulleys) over a single fixed pulley, grounding the reason in MA and energy conservation.

periods.teacher_notes: Having introduced MA conceptually, students now encounter their first concrete machine; the direction-change function of the fixed pulley is counterintuitive to students who expect all machines to reduce force. Watch for the error of thinking the movable pulley reduces the work done on the load — students must see that effort distance doubles as load distance halves, so work is constant. If a physical pulley is unavailable, a careful board diagram with numbered rope segments is sufficient for the counting argument.

periods.activity_title: Measuring Force on an Inclined Plane and Deriving MA = L/h
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram labelling effort F′ along length L, weight mg at height h, and the MA = L/h derivation

time_bands.activity: Ask: 'Would you rather carry a 20 kg box straight up a 1 m wall or roll it up a 4 m ramp?' Students predict which requires less force and state the trade-off: smaller force over greater distance. Introduce the inclined plane as a machine that exploits this trade-off.

Conduct Activity 7.3: prop the plank at three different angles (low, medium, steep). Students pull the cart up each angle with a spring balance, recording the force and the length of the plank used. They tabulate force vs. angle and observe the inverse relationship: shallower angle → smaller force → longer distance.

Derive MA = L/h on the board using work conservation: effort × L = weight × h, so MA = load/effort = L/h. Students apply this to the chapter's worked example (50 cm long ramp, 30 cm height, MA = 1.67) and verify with their own experimental readings from Activity 7.3.

Pause-and-Ponder: students reason why hill roads wind in gentle curves (longer path = smaller force needed per unit mass of vehicle) and why an inclined ladder is easier to climb than a vertical one. They connect both to MA = L/h, writing their reasoning in two sentences.

periods.teacher_notes: Connecting to the pulley's MA, the inclined plane shows that MA > 1 always requires a compensating increase in distance — a principle students should now articulate without prompting. The most common procedural error in Activity 7.3 is pulling the cart at an angle to the plank rather than parallel to it, which inflates the spring balance reading; remind students to keep the balance parallel to the surface. The hill-road Pause-and-Ponder makes the abstract MA formula directly relevant and is worth a few minutes of discussion.

periods.activity_title: Constructing a Lever, Deriving the Lever Principle, and Classifying Lever Types
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram of three lever classes with fulcrum, load, and effort positions labelled for each

time_bands.activity: Conduct Activity 7.4: students balance the ruler on the pencil, place the stapler close to the fulcrum, and add erasers at the far end until the ruler tips. They record the number of erasers needed at various stapler distances, observing that effort decreases as the effort arm lengthens.

Conduct Activity 7.5: build the beam balance, add coins to one cup, and adjust the other cup's distance from the fulcrum to balance. Students record effort force, effort arm, load force, and load arm in a table, then derive F₁ × d₁ = F₂ × d₂ from their data. Verify with the seesaw example: 15 kg at 2 m balances 30 kg at 1 m.

Draw the three lever-class diagrams on the board. Students classify: scissors (Class I), lemon squeezer (Class II), tweezers (Class III). For each class, students write which arm is longer (effort or load) and whether MA > 1, = 1, or < 1. They add two more everyday examples per class from their own experience.

Close the chapter's machine strand by returning to the energy-conservation constraint: F₁ × d₁ = F₂ × d₂ means work in = work out; machines only redistribute force and displacement, never create energy. Students address the final Pause-and-Ponder — why perpetual motion is impossible — writing one sentence linking it to energy dissipation through friction in any real machine.

periods.teacher_notes: Building on the pulley and inclined plane, the lever brings all three simple machines together under the single principle that work is conserved. The two activities require only classroom materials and run well simultaneously or sequentially in the same unit. A frequent classification error is placing the seesaw in Class II because the fulcrum is in the middle and children sit at the ends — clarify that the load is the child being lifted and the effort is the other child pressing down, making the fulcrum the point between them (Class I). The perpetual-motion close ties the entire machine strand back to the chapter's energy-conservation thread.
homework: A Class I lever has a load of 120 N placed 0.4 m from the fulcrum. Calculate the effort needed if the effort arm is 1.2 m, then identify one real-life Class I lever and explain why its effort arm is designed to be longer than its load arm.

coverage_handoff.section_label: 7.1 Work Done by a Constant Force
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students calculate work done using W = F × s, interpret the area under a force-displacement graph, and distinguish the scientific definition of work from everyday usage.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can apply a scalar product definition to compute work done from force and displacement values and read work from a force-displacement graph.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Work as F × s, SI unit joule, force-displacement graph area equals work

coverage_handoff.section_label: 7.1.1 When is work done equal to zero?
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students identify and justify the three conditions under which scientific work is zero, distinguishing between physiological effort and zero mechanical work.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can classify physical situations by the condition that makes work zero and explain the distinction between physical effort and scientific work.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Three zero-work conditions: zero force, zero displacement, force perpendicular to displacement

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students determine the sign of work done in force-displacement scenarios, including the goalkeeper example, and apply Newton's third law to identify paired positive and negative work.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can assign a sign to work done by identifying the relative directions of force and displacement and justify the result using the product rule.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Sign of work, goalkeeper 200 N over 15 cm giving −30 J, Newton's third law paired work

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students trace energy transfers through multi-object collisions using W = ΔE and apply Newton's third law to identify paired positive and negative work in a carrom-board sequence.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can apply the work-energy theorem to trace how energy transfers between objects in a sequence of interactions.
coverage_handoff.section_context: W = ΔE, energy as capacity to do work, carrom striker–coin–coin collision energy chain

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students classify everyday phenomena into seven named energy forms and construct conversion chains showing the transformation from one form to another.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can represent multi-step energy conversions as labelled chains naming the form, converting process, and resulting form.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Seven energy forms: mechanical, thermal, light, sound, electrical, nuclear, chemical; conversion examples

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students derive K = ½mv² from Newton's second law and kinematics, then apply it to calculate kinetic energy and solve reverse problems finding speed from work done.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can derive an energy expression from Newton's laws and kinematics and apply it to calculate kinetic energy or speed in novel contexts.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Derivation of K = ½mv² via v² = u² + 2as and W = F × s; worked examples including cricket ball and jet aircraft

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students investigate how drop height affects gravitational PE through Activity 7.1, then derive U = mgh using the work-energy theorem and calculate gravitational PE for a given mass and height.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can derive and apply a gravitational potential energy expression by connecting the work needed to raise a mass at constant speed to the energy stored.
coverage_handoff.section_context: U = mgh derivation via constant-speed lifting, Activity 7.1 sand depression, elastic and gravitational PE

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students verify energy conservation with a pendulum, prove ME = K + U = constant algebraically for free fall, and apply conservation to find speeds and distances in slide and truck-braking problems.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can apply conservation of mechanical energy to predict speed or distance in scenarios where only gravity acts, and identify where real shortfalls arise.
coverage_handoff.section_context: ME = K + U constant under gravity, pendulum Activity 7.2, slide speed v = √(2gh), truck ramp braking distance

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students define power as rate of work, estimate their own stair-climbing power, and solve problems involving power, work, and time for a weightlifter and an accelerating car.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can calculate power from work and time data and reason about how changing work or time affects the power required.
coverage_handoff.section_context: P = W/t, SI unit watt, weightlifter 300 W example, car accelerating to 72 km h⁻¹ in 10 s requiring 20 000 W

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students define effort, load, and mechanical advantage, compute MA for given scenarios, and articulate the energy-conservation constraint that machines do not create energy.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can compute mechanical advantage from effort and load values and explain why a machine with MA > 1 requires a compensating increase in effort distance.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Simple machines definition, effort and load, MA = load/effort, work conservation W_effort = W_load

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students measure effort for fixed and movable pulleys, compute MA for each, and verify that increased MA requires proportionally greater effort distance, keeping work constant.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can distinguish fixed from movable pulley systems by comparing their mechanical advantages and verify the energy-conservation constraint experimentally.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Fixed pulley MA = 1 direction change, movable pulley MA > 1, rope-segment count, elevator and crane applications

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students measure force at varying inclinations in Activity 7.3, derive MA = L/h from work conservation, and apply it to explain why shallower ramps and winding hill roads require less force.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can derive mechanical advantage for an inclined plane from work conservation and predict how changing slope angle affects the effort force required.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Inclined plane MA = L/h from F′ × L = mgh, Activity 7.3 spring balance at varied angles, hill-road application

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students derive F₁d₁ = F₂d₂ from Activities 7.4 and 7.5, classify levers into three classes with everyday examples, and connect all simple machines to the energy-conservation principle.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can derive the lever principle from work conservation, classify levers by fulcrum-load-effort arrangement, and calculate effort or load arm for a given scenario.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Lever principle F₁d₁ = F₂d₂, three lever classes with examples, beam balance Activity 7.5, perpetual motion impossibility

questions.section_label: 7.1 Work Done by a Constant Force
questions.implied_lo_assessed: Students can apply a scalar product definition to compute work done from force and displacement values and read work from a force-displacement graph.
questions.section_context: Work as F × s, SI unit joule, force-displacement graph area equals work

competency.competency_text: Defines work in scientific terms and represents the relationship between potential and kinetic energy (conservation of energy) in mathematical expressions.

questions.question_text: The table above shows the force acting on an object at two key displacement points, representing a constant-force scenario from 0 m to 3 m. What is the work done by this force over the 3 m displacement?

options.label: A
options.text: 3 J

options.label: B
options.text: 8 J

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student reads the force value (8 N) as the answer, confusing work with force and ignoring displacement.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student reads the displacement value (3 m) as the answer, confusing work with displacement and ignoring force.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student adds force and displacement (8 + 3 = 11) rather than multiplying, showing a procedural error in applying W = F × s.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the table format may be asked to redraw the force-displacement graph on paper and shade the rectangle to find area. Students who answer verbally can state the product rule aloud before computing.

questions.section_label: 7.1.1 When is work done equal to zero?
questions.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify physical situations by the condition that makes work zero and explain the distinction between physical effort and scientific work.
questions.section_context: Three zero-work conditions: zero force, zero displacement, force perpendicular to displacement

competency.competency_text: Defines work in scientific terms and represents the relationship between potential and kinetic energy (conservation of energy) in mathematical expressions.

questions.question_text: A student carries a heavy bag horizontally across a flat floor, holding it up with both arms. The student feels tired at the end. Which statement correctly explains how much scientific work is done on the bag?

options.label: A
options.text: Negative work is done on the bag because the student loses energy during the walk.

options.label: B
options.text: Positive work is done on the bag because the student exerts a real upward force on it.

options.label: C
options.text: Zero work is done because the student does not move.

options.label: D
options.text: Zero work is done on the bag because the upward force is perpendicular to the horizontal displacement.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student conflates exerting a real force with doing scientific work, not applying the direction condition of W = F × s.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student misidentifies the zero-displacement condition; the student does move horizontally, but displacement is not the bag's vertical displacement in this case — this reveals confusion about which displacement matters.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student imports the idea that the student loses internal energy (muscles tire) and incorrectly treats this as negative work done on the bag.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students may be invited to draw a force arrow (upward) and a displacement arrow (horizontal) on paper to see visually that they are perpendicular before selecting an answer. Those who express difficulty with 'perpendicular' can be prompted to describe where the force points and where the bag moves.

questions.implied_lo_assessed: Students can assign a sign to work done by identifying the relative directions of force and displacement and justify the result using the product rule.
questions.section_context: Sign of work, goalkeeper 200 N over 15 cm giving −30 J, Newton's third law paired work

competency.competency_text: Defines work in scientific terms and represents the relationship between potential and kinetic energy (conservation of energy) in mathematical expressions.

questions.question_text: A goalkeeper exerts a force of 200 N on an incoming football, bringing it to a stop over a displacement of 15 cm in the direction the ball was moving. (a) Calculate the work done by the goalkeeper on the ball, giving the correct sign and its unit. (b) Simultaneously, state the work done by the ball on the goalkeeper's hands, giving the sign and a reason using Newton's third law.
expected_elements: Converts 15 cm to 0.15 m before substituting into the formula.
Recognises force (200 N) and displacement (0.15 m) are in opposite directions, giving W = −(200 × 0.15) = −30 J.
States the work done by the ball on the goalkeeper is +30 J.

Justifies the positive sign by applying Newton's third law: the ball exerts an equal and opposite force on the goalkeeper's hands in the direction the goalkeeper's hands move (backwards), so force and displacement are in the same direction.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the sign convention may first draw arrows for force and displacement before computing. For part (b), students who have difficulty articulating Newton's third law may describe it as 'the ball pushes back on the goalkeeper' and receive partial credit if the direction reasoning is correct.

questions.implied_lo_assessed: Students can apply the work-energy theorem to trace how energy transfers between objects in a sequence of interactions.
questions.section_context: W = ΔE, energy as capacity to do work, carrom striker–coin–coin collision energy chain

competency.competency_text: Defines work in scientific terms and represents the relationship between potential and kinetic energy (conservation of energy) in mathematical expressions.

questions.question_text: A cricket ball bowled at high speed strikes a wicket. The ball slows down and the wicket is knocked over. Using W = ΔE and Newton's third law, trace the energy transfers in this event: explain who does positive work on whom, who does negative work on whom, and what happens to the energy of each object involved.
look_for: Identifies that the ball does positive work on the wicket (force in the direction of the wicket's displacement), so the wicket gains energy.
Identifies that the wicket does negative work on the ball (force on ball is opposite to ball's displacement), so the ball loses kinetic energy.
Uses W = ΔE explicitly to connect positive/negative work to energy gain/loss for each object.
Applies Newton's third law to explain that the ball and wicket exert equal and opposite forces on each other simultaneously, producing opposite-sign work.
Recognises that total energy is redistributed, not created or destroyed.

ECR.inclusivity: Students may use a diagram with labelled arrows rather than prose to show force and displacement directions for each object. Students who struggle to start may be prompted to first state what happens to the ball's speed and then reason backward using W = ΔE.

questions.implied_lo_assessed: Students can represent multi-step energy conversions as labelled chains naming the form, converting process, and resulting form.
questions.section_context: Seven energy forms: mechanical, thermal, light, sound, electrical, nuclear, chemical; conversion examples

competency.competency_text: Defines work in scientific terms and represents the relationship between potential and kinetic energy (conservation of energy) in mathematical expressions.

questions.question_text: A person eats food, uses their muscles to pedal a bicycle, and the bicycle bell rings when they press it. Which sequence correctly represents the energy conversions in this chain?

options.label: A
options.text: Chemical → Electrical → Sound

options.label: B
options.text: Chemical → Mechanical → Sound

options.label: C
options.text: Mechanical → Chemical → Sound

options.label: D
options.text: Thermal → Mechanical → Sound

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student reverses the first conversion, treating muscle movement as the starting energy form rather than the chemical energy stored in food.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student inserts electrical energy as an intermediate, confusing the food-to-muscle chain (which is chemical-to-mechanical) with an electrical appliance chain.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student begins with thermal energy, possibly confusing metabolic heat with the primary energy form in food (chemical energy).

MCQ.inclusivity: Students may annotate each step of the scenario (food eaten → muscles work → bell rings) with an energy form before selecting the sequence. Students who express uncertainty about 'chemical energy in food' can be prompted to recall what form of energy is stored in fuels and batteries.

questions.implied_lo_assessed: Students can derive an energy expression from Newton's laws and kinematics and apply it to calculate kinetic energy or speed in novel contexts.
questions.section_context: Derivation of K = ½mv² via v² = u² + 2as and W = F × s; worked examples including cricket ball and jet aircraft

competency.competency_text: Defines work in scientific terms and represents the relationship between potential and kinetic energy (conservation of energy) in mathematical expressions.

questions.question_text: A net force of 500 N acts on a 50 kg object at rest and brings it to a speed v over a displacement of 10 m. (a) Use W = F × s and W = ΔK = ½mv² (starting from rest) to calculate v. (b) If the same object were instead moving at 10 m s⁻¹ and the same net force acted over the same 10 m, explain without recalculating whether the final speed would be greater than, equal to, or less than your answer to part (a), and state why.
expected_elements: Calculates W = 500 × 10 = 5000 J.
Sets W = ½mv² = 5000 J with m = 50 kg, giving v² = 200, so v = √200 ≈ 14.1 m s⁻¹.
For part (b): the object already has kinetic energy (½ × 50 × 100 = 2500 J), so the same work adds to a non-zero initial KE, giving a larger final KE and therefore a larger final speed.
Correctly invokes W = ΔK = ½m(v² − u²) or equivalent reasoning rather than recomputing from scratch.

SCR.inclusivity: For part (a), students who are unsure of the algebraic route may be prompted to write W = ½mv² explicitly and then rearrange for v. For part (b), students may draw an energy bar chart (initial KE + work added = final KE) as an alternative to algebraic reasoning.

questions.implied_lo_assessed: Students can derive and apply a gravitational potential energy expression by connecting the work needed to raise a mass at constant speed to the energy stored.
questions.section_context: U = mgh derivation via constant-speed lifting, Activity 7.1 sand depression, elastic and gravitational PE

competency.competency_text: Defines work in scientific terms and represents the relationship between potential and kinetic energy (conservation of energy) in mathematical expressions.

questions.question_text: A 500 g ball is to be raised to a height of 8 m at constant speed. (a) Explain why the lifting force must equal mg and use this to derive that the potential energy stored equals mgh. (b) Calculate the gravitational potential energy gained by the ball (take g = 10 m s⁻²). (c) In Activity 7.1, a ball was dropped from 1 m and then from 2 m into loose sand. State what the deeper depression at the greater height indicates about the ball's potential energy before each drop.
expected_elements: States that constant speed means zero acceleration, so net force = 0, meaning lifting force = weight = mg.
Derives W = F × s = mg × h and equates this to PE gained: U = mgh.
Calculates U = 0.5 × 10 × 8 = 40 J.
States that the deeper depression from 2 m indicates the ball had greater gravitational PE at the greater height, consistent with U = mgh.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the constant-speed argument may be prompted with 'what does Newton's first law say about the forces on an object moving at constant speed?' before attempting the derivation. For part (c), students who have not conducted the activity may reason from the formula U = mgh alone.

questions.implied_lo_assessed: Students can apply conservation of mechanical energy to predict speed or distance in scenarios where only gravity acts, and identify where real shortfalls arise.
questions.section_context: ME = K + U constant under gravity, pendulum Activity 7.2, slide speed v = √(2gh), truck ramp braking distance

competency.competency_text: Defines work in scientific terms and represents the relationship between potential and kinetic energy (conservation of energy) in mathematical expressions.

questions.visual_stimulus:
Position | Height above ground (m) | Speed (m s⁻¹) | KE (J) | PE (J) | ME (J)
Top of slide (A) | 5 | 0 | ? | ? | ?
Midpoint (B) | 2 | ? | ? | ? | ?
Bottom (C) | 0 | ? | ? | ? | ?
Real bottom (C′) | 0 | 9 | ? | ? | ?
questions.task: A 4 kg ball is released from rest at the top of a slide 5 m above the ground. Using conservation of mechanical energy and the data table provided, complete the table and then evaluate whether the ball's motion on a real slide is consistent with conservation of mechanical energy.
questions.scaffold: Step 1 — Complete the 'ideal' rows (A, B, C): use ME = K + U = constant. At A, all energy is PE; at C, all is KE. At B, split ME between KE and PE using the heights given. Take g = 10 m s⁻². Step 2 — For the real bottom row (C′): the ball's measured speed is 9 m s⁻¹. Calculate the actual KE and ME at C′ and compare with the ideal ME at A. Step 3 — Write two or three sentences: (a) state whether ME is conserved in the real case and by how much it differs, (b) identify which form(s) of energy account for the missing energy, and (c) evaluate the claim that conservation of mechanical energy is violated in this experiment.
format_of_output: Completed data table with all KE, PE, and ME values filled in for positions A, B, C (ideal), and C′ (real).
Written evaluation of two to three sentences addressing the three prompts in Step 3.

OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The section's central activity is tracking KE and PE at multiple positions; a data table with a real vs. ideal comparison directly operationalises the implied_lo's evaluation demand.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether students can apply ME = K + U to compute values at multiple heights and critically evaluate a real experimental result against the ideal conservation principle.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Step 1 checks procedural application of ME conservation; Step 2 introduces the real-world deviation; Step 3 requires evaluation — students who complete Steps 1–2 correctly but attribute the shortfall to 'the formula being wrong' have not reached the evaluation level.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: correct ME at each position; correctly computes real KE at C′ as ½×4×81 = 162 J vs. ideal 200 J; attributes 38 J difference to friction and air resistance; explicitly states ME conservation holds as a principle but is masked by energy transfer to thermal form. Weak: completes the table but states 'conservation is violated'; or attributes shortfall to measurement error without identifying the energy form.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who struggle with simultaneous KE and PE may complete the table one column at a time (all KE first, then all PE). Students who prefer a graphical representation may draw a bar chart of KE and PE at each position as a supplement to the written evaluation.

questions.implied_lo_assessed: Students can calculate power from work and time data and reason about how changing work or time affects the power required.
questions.section_context: P = W/t, SI unit watt, weightlifter 300 W example, car accelerating to 72 km h⁻¹ in 10 s requiring 20 000 W

competency.competency_text: Defines work in scientific terms and represents the relationship between potential and kinetic energy (conservation of energy) in mathematical expressions.

questions.question_text: Two workers carry identical loads up the same staircase. Worker A takes 20 seconds; Worker B takes 40 seconds. Which statement correctly compares their work done and power?

options.label: A
options.text: Both do the same work; Worker A uses twice the power of Worker B.

options.label: B
options.text: Both use the same power because they carry the same load.

options.label: C
options.text: Worker A does more work because they finish faster.

options.label: D
options.text: Worker B does more work because they take longer.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student conflates speed of completion with work done, thinking faster implies more work — does not separate work (force × displacement) from power (work/time).
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student confuses 'same load' with 'same power', ignoring the time variable in P = W/t.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student thinks longer time means more work, reversing the independence of work from time; confuses duration with effort.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students may be asked to write the formula P = W/t and substitute numbers for a hypothetical load (e.g., W = 100 J) before selecting. Students who respond verbally can explain the staircase scenario in their own words to demonstrate understanding.

questions.implied_lo_assessed: Students can compute mechanical advantage from effort and load values and explain why a machine with MA > 1 requires a compensating increase in effort distance.
questions.section_context: Simple machines definition, effort and load, MA = load/effort, work conservation W_effort = W_load

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates the principle of mechanical advantage by constructing simple machines (system of levers and pulleys).

questions.question_text: A simple machine lifts a 300 N load using an effort of 100 N. A student claims: 'This machine creates extra force from nothing.' Which response correctly evaluates this claim?

options.label: A
options.text: The claim is correct; machines with MA > 1 always create net energy.

options.label: B
options.text: The claim is correct; the machine reduces both the force and the work required.

options.label: C
options.text: The claim is wrong; a machine with MA > 1 must always reduce the load's displacement to zero.

options.label: D
options.text: The claim is wrong; MA = 3 means the effort moves three times the distance the load moves, so total work is the same on both sides.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student holds the fundamental misconception that MA > 1 implies energy creation — has not connected MA to the compensating distance increase.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student correctly identifies the claim is wrong but offers an implausible mechanical consequence, showing a partial understanding of work conservation without correctly identifying the distance trade-off.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student conflates force reduction with work reduction, not recognising that work = force × distance and the distance compensates for the force reduction.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students may be asked to compute work on both sides using a made-up distance (e.g., load moves 1 m) before evaluating the claim. Students who struggle with the concept verbally may draw arrows showing effort arm and load arm lengths.

questions.implied_lo_assessed: Students can distinguish fixed from movable pulley systems by comparing their mechanical advantages and verify the energy-conservation constraint experimentally.
questions.section_context: Fixed pulley MA = 1 direction change, movable pulley MA > 1, rope-segment count, elevator and crane applications

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates the principle of mechanical advantage by constructing simple machines (system of levers and pulleys).

questions.question_text: A movable pulley system uses two rope segments to support a load of 80 N. (a) Calculate the effort force required and the mechanical advantage. (b) If the load is raised by 0.5 m, calculate how far the effort end of the rope must be pulled, and verify that work done by effort equals work done on the load. (c) Explain in one sentence why a fixed pulley is still useful even though its MA = 1.
expected_elements: Two rope segments supporting the load means each carries half the load: effort = 80/2 = 40 N; MA = 80/40 = 2.
Load rises 0.5 m; effort rope must be pulled 2 × 0.5 = 1.0 m (twice the load distance).
Work by effort = 40 × 1.0 = 40 J; work on load = 80 × 0.5 = 40 J; both are equal, confirming energy conservation.
A fixed pulley changes the direction of the applied force (e.g., allows pulling down instead of lifting up), making the task more convenient even without a force reduction.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the rope-segment argument may be prompted to draw the pulley with two rope segments and label the tension in each. For part (b), students may verify the work equality by working backward from the energy equation before computing distances.

questions.implied_lo_assessed: Students can derive mechanical advantage for an inclined plane from work conservation and predict how changing slope angle affects the effort force required.
questions.section_context: Inclined plane MA = L/h from F′ × L = mgh, Activity 7.3 spring balance at varied angles, hill-road application

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates the principle of mechanical advantage by constructing simple machines (system of levers and pulleys).

questions.visual_stimulus:
Plank length L (cm) | Height h (cm) | Effort force F′ (N) | Weight of cart mg (N) | MA = L/h | Work by effort (J) | Work on load (J)
60 | 30 | 5.0 | 10 | ? | ? | ?
80 | 30 | 3.75 | 10 | ? | ? | ?
120 | 30 | 2.5 | 10 | ? | ? | ?
questions.question_text: The table shows results from Activity 7.3, where a toy cart was pulled up planks of different lengths but the same height. Complete the table and answer the questions below.
expected_elements: Row 1: MA = 60/30 = 2; Work by effort = 5.0 × 0.60 = 3.0 J; Work on load = 10 × 0.30 = 3.0 J.
Row 2: MA = 80/30 ≈ 2.67; Work by effort = 3.75 × 0.80 = 3.0 J; Work on load = 10 × 0.30 = 3.0 J.
Row 3: MA = 120/30 = 4; Work by effort = 2.5 × 1.20 = 3.0 J; Work on load = 10 × 0.30 = 3.0 J.
States that as plank length increases (shallower angle), effort force decreases but distance over which it acts increases, keeping work constant.
Connects to MA = L/h: greater L for the same h gives greater MA and smaller effort force required.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who struggle with unit conversion may be prompted to convert all lengths to metres before computing work. Students who complete the table but cannot articulate the pattern may be asked: 'What changes in each row, and what stays the same?'

questions.implied_lo_assessed: Students can derive the lever principle from work conservation, classify levers by fulcrum-load-effort arrangement, and calculate effort or load arm for a given scenario.
questions.section_context: Lever principle F₁d₁ = F₂d₂, three lever classes with examples, beam balance Activity 7.5, perpetual motion impossibility

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates the principle of mechanical advantage by constructing simple machines (system of levers and pulleys).

questions.question_text: A seesaw has its fulcrum at the centre. Child A (mass 15 kg) sits 2 m from the fulcrum on one side. Child B (mass 30 kg) sits on the other side. (a) Use the lever principle F₁d₁ = F₂d₂ to calculate how far from the fulcrum Child B must sit for the seesaw to balance. (b) Identify the class of lever the seesaw represents, stating the positions of the fulcrum, load, and effort. (c) A student says: 'If I use a longer effort arm, the lever does more work for me.' Use the work-conservation principle to evaluate this claim.
expected_elements: Takes weight of Child A = 15 × 10 = 150 N; weight of Child B = 30 × 10 = 300 N.
Applies 150 × 2 = 300 × d₂, giving d₂ = 1 m.
Classifies the seesaw as a Class I lever: fulcrum is between the load (Child B being lifted) and the effort (Child A pressing down).

Evaluates the claim as incorrect: a longer effort arm reduces the effort force required but increases the distance the effort moves; by F₁d₁ = F₂d₂, total work is conserved — the lever does not create extra work.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the lever principle algebraically may draw the seesaw with forces and distances labelled before substituting. For part (c), students who respond with 'it makes the work easier' rather than 'it does the same work' may be prompted to define 'easier' in terms of force and distance before revising their evaluation.
